questions.q: What does REPEATABLE READ guarantee, beyond what READ COMMITTED guarantees?
options: If you read a row once in a transaction, reading the same row again in the same transaction returns the same value
Every query automatically retries until it succeeds
No other session can ever read the same table at the same time
New rows can never be inserted into the database while the transaction is open
questions.explain: REPEATABLE READ prevents the nonrepeatable read anomaly: a row you've already read cannot be changed by another transaction until yours finishes.

questions.q: How does REPEATABLE READ actually enforce that guarantee?
options: It uses range locks on every possible predicate
It disables all other sessions' transactions until this one commits
It takes a snapshot of the entire database at the start of the transaction
It holds shared locks on every row it has read until the transaction ends, instead of releasing them after each statement
questions.explain: The core mechanical difference from READ COMMITTED is lock duration: REPEATABLE READ keeps shared locks for the whole transaction, not just each statement.

questions.q: What anomaly does REPEATABLE READ still allow?
options: Dirty reads
Nonrepeatable reads
None -- REPEATABLE READ prevents all three anomalies
Phantom reads
questions.explain: REPEATABLE READ only locks rows it has already read -- it has no mechanism to stop a brand-new row from being inserted that matches the query's criteria.

questions.q: In the nonrepeatable-read timeline, what happens differently if Session A runs under REPEATABLE READ instead of READ COMMITTED?
options: Session A automatically sees Session B's change reflected in its first read
Session B's UPDATE blocks until Session A's transaction commits or rolls back, instead of committing immediately
Session A's first SELECT fails with an error
Session B's UPDATE still commits immediately, with no change in behavior
questions.explain: Because REPEATABLE READ holds its shared lock on the row Session A already read, Session B's UPDATE must wait for that lock to be released.

questions.q: What is the concurrency cost of REPEATABLE READ compared to READ COMMITTED?
options: REPEATABLE READ prevents all other sessions from reading any table at all
There is no cost -- REPEATABLE READ performs identically to READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ actually reduces blocking compared to READ COMMITTED
Other sessions trying to write to rows you've read must wait longer, for as long as your transaction stays open
questions.explain: Holding locks for the whole transaction, rather than releasing them after each statement, means other sessions' writes to those rows block for longer.
